summary: Gives guidelines for sending documents that follow the US Department of Defense standard MIL-STD-1840 through Internet email. It defines how that kind of data is labeled with a MIME content type. It is informational only.

plainLanguage.summary: Some government paperwork came in a special format. This note explains how to tuck that paperwork into an email and label it so the receiver knows what it is.

questions: how to send mil-std-1840 files by email
subtitle: Mailing military technical documents through email

tldr.problem: The US Department of Defense standard MIL-STD-1840 for exchanging technical data was designed for 9-track tape, but email provides a more convenient transport mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new MIME content type called Application/CALS-1840 that wraps MIL-STD-1840 formatted data so it can be sent via Internet email while preserving the original file structure.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now exchange MIL-STD-1840 data via email without converting the format, preserving compatibility with existing processing software.

today: RFC 1895 is an Informational RFC and has not been superseded. It remains the specification for exchanging MIL-STD-1840 data via Internet email.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MIL-STD-1840 is the United States Department of Defense standard for exchanging digital data. Traditionally, this data was transported on 9-track magnetic tape, but email offers a more convenient mechanism for many applications. The Application/CALS-1840 MIME media type enables MIL-STD-1840 data exchanges using Internet email as the transport mechanism instead of physical media.

This RFC was reviewed and authorized by the Continuous Acquisition and Life-cycle Support (CALS) Industry Steering Group, which guides the development of CALS standards including MIL-STD-1840.
sections.plainLanguage: The military needed a way to send technical blueprints and documents through email. This RFC explains how to do that using a special label.

sections.title: MIL-STD-1840 Data Structure
sections.content:
An MIL-STD-1840 exchange consists of a set of files with well-defined file names. Each set contains a declaration file (which describes the contents) followed by one or more data files. The data files contain header records immediately followed by the actual data, which may be formatted according to published specifications or contractual agreements.

Rather than transforming 1840 files into separate MIME body parts, the RFC preserves the 1840 file format as-is. This approach has three advantages: many file types used in 1840 are not registered MIME types; there is existing software capable of reading 1840 formatted files; and three revisions of the standard have maintained the same file structure, so a single processor may handle any revision.
sections.plainLanguage: A military document set has a cover sheet that lists what's inside, then the actual documents. We keep them in their original military format instead of changing them for email.

sections.title: MIME Implementation
sections.content:
A set of related files constitutes a transfer unit in MIL-STD-1840, and each transfer unit shall correspond to a Multipart/Mixed MIME entity. The declaration file must be the first body part in the Multipart/Mixed entity. Several transfer units may be included in a single MIME message, and each Application/CALS-1840 body part requires two parameters: filename and version.

The filename parameter gives the transfer unit filename as defined by the military standard. The filename has a specific syntax: it begins with the letter D, followed by a three-character transfer unit sequence, optionally followed by a type letter and a three-character data file sequence. All Application/CALS-1840 body parts in a single Multipart/Mixed entity must share the same transfer unit sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send the military documents through email, you group them together and put a special label on each one that says what version of the military standard it uses.

sections.title: Version Parameter and Example
sections.content:
The version parameter indicates which version of MIL-STD-1840 the data conforms to. Valid values include MIL-STD-1840C, MIL-STD-1840B (dated 19921103), and MIL-STD-1840A (dated 19871222). Each revision maintains the same fundamental file structure, allowing processing software to handle data from multiple versions.

The RFC includes a complete example showing a single transfer unit with three data files: a declaration file, a contract-defined file, and an IGES file. The headers and data conform to MIL-STD-1840B, and the content is base64 encoded for email transmission. This example demonstrates how a real military data exchange would be packaged for email delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the receiver which version of the military standard you used, so they know what software to use to read it.
